title: The EPA wants to make data centre pollution disclosure optional
summary:
The US Environmental Protection Agency has proposed making public disclosure of air pollution from minor sources voluntary rather than mandatory, a change that would cover the diesel generators clustered around data centres.
It follows the same direction as the exemptions the administration has already granted, having excused data centres and rockets from parts of environmental law earlier this year.
How data centres come to be minor sources at all is the part worth understanding.
The region holds roughly 10,500 diesel generators at data centres with a combined capacity approaching 27 gigawatts, which is a fleet of fossil generation assembled without ever being permitted as a power station.
Backup generation is what allows a data centre to be built faster than the grid serving it, and a disclosure regime that becomes optional removes the main mechanism by which anyone downwind finds out.

Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported that 260 of the 558 missing people in Tibet were foreigners and two villagers were rescued.
The disaster in Nepal and Tibet is not a one-off.

title: These Cookies Are 3D-Printed and Made of Recycled Plastic
summary:
They’ve genetically engineered yeast to transform PET plastic and agricultural waste into a vanilla-flavored protein cookie that they think could be a solution to both plastic pollution and food shortages.
For microbiologists at Southern Illinois University Carbondale, the solution lay in converting plastic and plant waste into “edible, protein-rich supplements.”Their concoction — snack-sized morsels called “µBites” (pronounced “microbites”) — didn’t end up winning the Deep Space Food Challenge.
Lahiru Jayakody, who led the project, holds one of the 3D-printed, plastic-derived cookies.
“The way to address that, I believe, is by using microbes.”At this early stage, these cookies are also very expensive.
Convincing the public to accept and eat plastic-derived cookies made from trash, on the other hand, is a challenge that may take more than science to solve.

title: Australia is preparing to impose its data centre energy rules over Queensland’s objection
summary:
The policy requires large facilities to buy power from newly built renewable projects rather than drawing on the existing grid.
Energy Minister Chris Bowen has indicated the Commonwealth will legislate federal standards whether or not the states sign up.
Energy regulation in Australia has historically run through cooperative arrangements between the Commonwealth and the states, and a federal law reaching directly into state energy markets would be tested.
A requirement to buy power from new renewable projects only works if those projects can be built and connected on the timeline the data centres need.
Australia is not doing this in isolation, and the alternative to writing rules is visible elsewhere.

title: Cornish residents urged to "join in" with food waste drive
summary:
Understanding the benefits of recycling food waste could encourage more people to do it in future, Cornwall Council has said.
For the past two years, leftover food has been able to be taken to an anaerobic digester to be converted into methane to generate electricity and produce fertiliser.
The council said about 36,000 tonnes of food waste had been recycled to date since the introduction of its new waste service.
It said it hoped increased participation through understanding the benefits would help meet its target to recycle nearly two-thirds of Cornwall's waste by 2029.

title: The US Army is betting on nuclear microreactors to keep its bases powered even if the grid goes dark
summary:
The US Army announced plans to build nuclear microreactors on five military bases as it tests whether nuclear energy can keep critical operations running if the power grid goes down.
The Army sees the technology as a potential way to ensure bases and troops can operate off-grid during a conflict.
Questions remain about the ultimate cost, which vendors will prove viable, and how widely the Army could deploy the reactors.
Army Secretary Dan Driscoll said the contracts are meant to give bases reliable power independent of potentially vulnerable external commercial grids.
Nuclear microreactors are small nuclear reactors that generate power through nuclear fission on a smaller scale.

title: Scottish Highlands benefiting from 'coolcation' trend
summary:
James MacLeod, concierge at the Glencoe House Hotel, in the Scottish Highlands, is talking about how he has noticed a big shift in visitors' perceptions.
Climate change is redrawing Europe's summer tourism map.
Wildfires, droughts and record-breaking heatwaves are making summer months increasingly uncomfortable and unpredictable across southern Europe.
By contrast, Scotland and other northern European nations are finding themselves perfectly positioned to offer a "coolcation" escape.
Within the UK, holiday rental website Cottages.com said that its Scottish portfolio has been the most viewed this summer.

title: Government invests £71m to help reopen Devon tungsten mine
summary:
More than £70m of public money will be invested into a mining company to help restart production, the chancellor has said.
The Hemerdon tungsten and tin mine in Devon will receive up to £71m from the National Wealth Fund to resume operations at the mine near Plymouth.
Chancellor John Healey said it meant Britain could tap into one of the world's largest deposit of the mineral which is used in steel, electronics and aerospace industries.
The government said it would ringfence 50% of the production for use in Britain.
The financing consists of a £36m equity investment alongside up to £35m of lending to help Tungsten West restart production.

title: Spain wants data centres on 80% renewables every hour, or no grid connection
summary:
Spain has drafted a decree that would require new data centres to source at least 80% of their electricity from renewables in every hour of operation, with loss of grid connection as the penalty for failing to comply.
The hourly requirement is the technically demanding part.
Every new megawatt requires matching renewable installations to be in place within 18 months before operation, achieved either through contracts or by building locally.
Developers who priced their models on annual renewable matching would have to redo the arithmetic or walk away from a queue position that took years to obtain.
Consultation is where the industry gets to argue, and the hourly matching requirement is the clause it will argue about.

title: Less than 300 million barrels left: the engineering limits threatening the American Strategic Petroleum Reserve
summary:
As crude inventories in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve drain toward their operational limits, America is left, armed with just 300 million barrels.
Consequently, the total volume of fluid inside the reserve must be permanently maintained at 714 million barrels.
But while 70 million barrels is the structural floor where the salt rock might physically hold together, the practical operational floor is much higher, around 250 million barrels.
Under the Energy Policy and Conservation Act, federal law places a strict statutory stop at 252.4 million barrels.
With an inventory of roughly 293 million barrels, only about 41 million barrels remain before hitting the 252 million-barrel statutory limit.

title: Michael Sheen toxic waste documentary 'the tip of the iceberg'
summary:
A former Monsanto worker who spent three years helping seal toxic waste underground said staff had "cheap" protective equipment and were not told what they were burying.
Stephen Constance worked at the chemical giant's Newport factory in the 1990s and came forward after the BBC documentary Buried with Michael Sheen highlighted Wales' toxic waste legacy.
But the 14 sites identified in the programme are just the tip of the iceberg and there are about 20,000 high-concern sites in the UK, said Dr David Megson, the scientist involved in the documentary.
Eastman Chemical Company, which is responsible for Monsanto's legacy production in the UK, did not respond when asked to comment.
Constance was one of dozens of people who contacted BBC Wales after coverage of Sheen's investigation into Monsanto and the dumping of polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs).

summary:
Hundreds of travellers are missing, including at least 291 foreign tourists, after a flash flood swept away buildings on the Nepal-Tibet border.
Aerial footage showed multi-storey buildings partially submerged by the muddy floodwaters, and a valley filled with dust and smoke.
Nepal's foreign minister says preliminary reports show it may have been caused by an earthquake triggering an avalanche, which lead to flash floods.
China's President Xi Jinping is urging "all-out" search efforts for the missing, as well as stronger monitoring and early warning systems to prevent secondary disasters.
